title: Artificially Induced Mismatch training (AIM) - Mechanisms of effective motor learning
summary:
After a stroke, the brain has a particularly strong capacity to regain lost movement abilities through learning for several weeks; thereafter, this readiness to learn declines markedly. This study investigates whether a comparable state of heightened learning readiness can be induced artificially. The underlying assumption is that a sustained mismatch between an executed movement and its visual feedback that cannot be reduced through adaptation destabilizes existing motor programs and thereby facilitates subsequent motor learning.
Healthy young adults, healthy older adults, and people in the chronic phase after ischemic stroke are studied. Within each of these three cohorts, 60 participants are randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to one of three VR-based training conditions: mismatch learning, conventional error-based learning, or a very easy, low-error control condition. Thus, 20 participants per training arm and cohort, and 180 participants overall, are planned. Each participant takes part in only one training arm and completes one block of five training days, with 90 minutes of training per day. At the end of the training block, a standardized adaptation task is used to determine how rapidly performance improves.
The primary measure is the exponential learning-rate parameter `α`; higher values indicate faster motor adaptation. Transfer to other motor tasks and changes in brain activity and functional connectivity are assessed as secondary outcomes. The study also examines whether the effect of mismatch training is related to age, motor impairment, and structural and functional characteristics of the brain

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Adult participants aged at least 18 years who are able to provide informed consent. Healthy young participants, healthy older participants, and patients in the chronic phase after first-ever ischemic stroke with mild to moderate persistent hemiparesis are eligible. Right-handedness is required. Stroke patients must have sufficient cognitive function to provide written informed consent and comply with the study requirements. Stroke patients must have had a unilateral, first-ever ischemic stroke at least 6 months before study inclusion.
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion criteria include contraindications to MRI or MEG, severe visual impairment, or inability to provide informed consent. In the healthy control groups, pre-existing functional impairment of the upper extremity and known neurological or psychiatric disorders are exclusion criteria. Additional exclusion criteria for stroke patients include cerebellar infarction, hemorrhagic stroke, severe aphasia, severe apraxia or severe neglect, post-stroke epilepsy, relevant skull or brain lesions outside the defined stroke event, and other neurological or psychiatric disorders that may interfere with study participation or data interpretation.
